items.title: Linear capillary free-surface model
items.design_state: Step 1 complete draft; readiness recorded separately.
items.statement:
Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval, with absolute time $t\in I$ in seconds, and let $E$ be an oriented three-dimensional Euclidean affine space: its translation vectors form an oriented three-dimensional Euclidean vector space, and no origin is distinguished. The adopted Newtonian spacetime is the product $I\times E$. Define $\mathrm{SO}(3):=\{Q\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}:Q^{\mathsf T}Q=I_3,\ \det Q=1\}$. A classical Cartesian inertial chart on $I\times E$ is the event-coordinate map $(t,X)\mapsto(t,\mathbf r_t(X))$, where there are a fixed $t_{\rm ref}\in I$, an orientation-preserving affine isometry $\mathbf r_{t_{\rm ref}}:E\to\mathbb R^3$ whose linear part lies in $\mathrm{SO}(3)$, and a constant $w\in\mathbb R^3$ in metres per second such that $\mathbf r_t(X)=\mathbf r_{t_{\rm ref}}(X)+w(t-t_{\rm ref})$ for every $t\in I$ and $X\in E$. Thus each fixed-time spatial coordinate map is an orientation-preserving affine isometry, and its coordinates are measured in metres. Inertial charts are related by $t^*=t+t_0$ and $\mathbf r^*=Q\mathbf r+vt+a$, where $t_0$ is a constant time translation in seconds, $Q\in\mathrm{SO}(3)$ is constant, $v\in\mathbb R^3$ is constant in metres per second, and $a\in\mathbb R^3$ is constant in metres. Thus “frame” means this adapted event-coordinate map on Newtonian spacetime, not an observer congruence or a basis field. Write the selected chart coordinates as $(x_1,x_2,z)$, with horizontal coordinate $x=(x_1,x_2)$ and upward vertical coordinate $z$, all in metres, and let $e_z$ be the upward unit vector.

Fix $h>0$ metres and horizontal periods $L_1,L_2>0$ metres; set $\mathbb T^2_L:=\mathbb R^2/(L_1\mathbb Z\times L_2\mathbb Z)$. For a scalar or vector field $f$ on $\mathbb T^2_L$, its lift is $\widetilde f(\widetilde x):=f([\widetilde x])$ on $\mathbb R^2$ and is periodic under each lattice translation $(L_1n_1,L_2n_2)$, $n_1,n_2\in\mathbb Z$. The notation $C^r$ for fields on $\mathbb T^2_L\times I$ or $\mathbb T^2_L\times[-h,0]\times I$ means that the lifted field has continuous ordinary coordinate partial derivatives through total order $r$, with derivatives at $z=-h,0$ understood as continuous one-sided extensions. Horizontal coordinate partial derivatives are the corresponding derivatives of the periodic lift, so they are independent of the representative of a torus point. The flat reference liquid region is $\Omega_0:=\mathbb T^2_L\times(-h,0)$; the bottom $z=-h$ is a fixed solid bed and the real first-order surface-displacement coefficient is $\eta:\mathbb T^2_L\times I\to\mathbb R$, in metres. It is a formal perturbation coefficient, with no amplitude restriction such as $\eta>-h$. For an optional finite-displacement geometric interpretation on a compact time interval $K\subset I$, introduce a dimensionless $\varepsilon>0$ and the graph $z=\varepsilon\eta(x,t)$. Continuity on the compact horizontal cell times $K$ bounds $|\eta|$ by some finite $M$, so choosing $\varepsilon M<h$ keeps that graph above the bed. This geometric scaling imposes no bound on the formal coefficient and asserts no nonlinear solution or approximation accuracy. Horizontal periodic faces are mathematical identifications, not physical walls.

Adopt a homogeneous single-component liquid with constant mass density $\rho>0$ in kilograms per cubic metre, constant downward gravitational acceleration $-g e_z$ with $g>0$ in metres per second squared, and constant surface-tension coefficient $\gamma>0$ in newtons per metre, equivalently kilograms per second squared. Here $\rho$, $g$, $\gamma$, and the constant gas pressure $p_a$ in pascals are primitive inputs of this formulation; $h,L_1,L_2$ are fixed geometric parameters. For the optional finite-displacement geometry on $K$, define $\mathcal Q_{\ell,\varepsilon}:=\{(x,z,t):x\in\mathbb T^2_L,\ t\in K,\ -h<z<\varepsilon\eta(x,t)\}$. If an auxiliary liquid-pressure field $p_{\ell,\varepsilon}:\mathcal Q_{\ell,\varepsilon}\to\mathbb R$ in pascals is supplied, its liquid-side interface trace, when it exists, is $p_{\ell,\varepsilon}^\Gamma(x,t):=\lim_{z\uparrow\varepsilon\eta(x,t)}p_{\ell,\varepsilon}(x,z,t)$. No extension or smoothness of this pressure across the interface is assumed. The gas is modeled only by the prescribed constant pressure $p_a$; no gas momentum equation is included. This optional geometric pressure is distinct from the formal first-order pressure coefficient used below. The reduced first-order model does not construct such a nonlinear pressure family and has no independent pressure evolution equation. Its independent fields are the unrestricted formal displacement coefficient $\eta$ in metres and the scalar velocity-potential coefficient $\phi$ in metres squared per second, both on the fixed reference geometry. Define the full Cartesian gradient by $\nabla\phi:=(\partial_{x_1}\phi,\partial_{x_2}\phi,\partial_z\phi)$ and the derived fluid-velocity vector field by $u:=\nabla\phi:\mathbb T^2_L\times[-h,0]\times I\to\mathbb R^3$, in metres per second; there is no additive uniform velocity component. With $u=(u_1,u_2,u_3)$, define $\operatorname{div}u:=\partial_{x_1}u_1+\partial_{x_2}u_2+\partial_z u_3$ and $\operatorname{curl}u:=(\partial_{x_2}u_3-\partial_z u_2,\partial_z u_1-\partial_{x_1}u_3,\partial_{x_1}u_2-\partial_{x_2}u_1)$ using these Cartesian derivatives on the lifts. The model is inviscid, meaning no viscous-stress or viscous-dissipation terms are included; it is incompressible and irrotational, meaning $\operatorname{div}u=0$ and $\operatorname{curl}u=0$. On the torus this potential assumption is stronger than irrotationality alone, since a curl-free field need not be the gradient of a periodic scalar. Assume $\phi$ is at least $C^3$ and $\eta$ is at least $C^2$ in the periodic-lift sense just defined; derivatives below are classical.

Set $\nabla_h:=(\partial_{x_1},\partial_{x_2})$ and $\Delta_h:=\partial_{x_1}^2+\partial_{x_2}^2$ on the periodic lifts. For a horizontal vector field $v=(v_1,v_2)$, define $\nabla_h\cdot v:=\partial_{x_1}v_1+\partial_{x_2}v_2$ and $|v|^2:=v_1^2+v_2^2$. For the optional graph $z=\varepsilon\eta(x,t)$, the outward normal from liquid to gas is $n_\varepsilon:=(-\varepsilon\nabla_h\eta,1)/\sqrt{1+\varepsilon^2|\nabla_h\eta|^2}$ and the signed curvature is $\kappa_\varepsilon:=-\nabla_h\cdot(\varepsilon\nabla_h\eta/\sqrt{1+\varepsilon^2|\nabla_h\eta|^2})$, in inverse metres. The geometric liquid-minus-gas pressure law, whenever this optional pressure and trace are supplied, is $p_{\ell,\varepsilon}^\Gamma-p_a=\gamma\kappa_\varepsilon$. Its formal first-order curvature coefficient is $-\Delta_h\eta$. On the fixed reference slab define the first-order pressure coefficient $p^{(1)}:=-\rho\phi_t$, in pascals, in the potential gauge encoded by the dynamic equation below. The first-order interface pressure balance at the reference plane is $p^{(1)}(x,0,t)-\rho g\eta=-\gamma\Delta_h\eta$: the term $-\rho g\eta$ is the hydrostatic reference pressure evaluated to first order at height $\varepsilon\eta$. Substituting $p^{(1)}(x,0,t)=-\rho\phi_t(x,0,t)$ gives exactly the displayed linear dynamic condition. All coefficients are evaluated at $z=0$; neither $\phi$ nor its velocity is evaluated at $z=\varepsilon\eta$ or outside the fixed slab. At the fixed bed impose only impermeability, meaning zero normal fluid velocity, $u_z=0$, equivalently $\phi_z=0$ at $z=-h$. Since the bed is fixed, no-slip would additionally impose $u=0$ there; that condition is not imposed in this inviscid branch. The first-order kinematic equation below encodes surface motion at the reference plane; it is not a solid-wall condition or a claim of nonlinear material motion for the optional graph.

The selected first-order model is defined by retaining only terms linear in perturbations about the hydrostatic rest state $\eta=0$, $u=0$, and reference pressure $p_a-\rho g z$, then evaluating surface derivatives at $z=0$. Products of perturbations are discarded, with no error estimate for replacing a finite-amplitude flow by this linear model. On $\Omega_0\times I$ the adopted equations and boundary conditions are

$$\Delta_h\phi+\partial_z^2\phi=0,\qquad -h<z<0,$$

$$\partial_z\phi(x,-h,t)=0,$$

$$\partial_t\eta(x,t)=\partial_z\phi(x,0,t),\qquad \partial_t\phi(x,0,t)+g\eta(x,t)-\frac{\gamma}{\rho}\Delta_h\eta(x,t)=0.$$

These are model assumptions for the stated idealized regime. They assert no existence or uniqueness for the nonlinear free-boundary equations, no finite-amplitude approximation bound, and no empirical claim that a particular liquid satisfies this model.

items.physical_scope: Adopted first-order inviscid, homogeneous, incompressible and irrotational capillary-gravity waves in a periodic horizontal cell above a fixed impermeable bed, with constant density and surface tension and negligible air inertia. No viscosity, background current, finite-amplitude accuracy, solvability, or universal empirical validity is asserted.

items.title: Linear capillary-gravity wave dispersion
items.design_state: Step 1 complete draft; readiness recorded separately.
items.statement:
Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval, with absolute time $t\in I$ measured in seconds, and let $E$ be an oriented three-dimensional Euclidean affine space: its translation vectors form an oriented three-dimensional Euclidean vector space and no origin is distinguished. The Newtonian spacetime is $I\times E$. Define $\mathrm{SO}(3):=\{Q\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}:Q^{\mathsf T}Q=I_3,\ \det Q=1\}$. A Cartesian inertial chart is the event-coordinate map $(t,X)\mapsto(t,\mathbf r_t(X))$ for which, at some fixed $t_{\rm ref}\in I$, $\mathbf r_{t_{\rm ref}}:E\to\mathbb R^3$ is an orientation-preserving affine isometry whose linear part lies in $\mathrm{SO}(3)$ and $\mathbf r_t(X)=\mathbf r_{t_{\rm ref}}(X)+w(t-t_{\rm ref})$ for a constant $w\in\mathbb R^3$ in metres per second. Thus each fixed-time spatial map is an orientation-preserving affine isometry; inertial charts are related by $t^*=t+t_0$ and $\mathbf r^*=Q\mathbf r+vt+a$, with constant $t_0$ in seconds, $Q\in\mathrm{SO}(3)$, $v\in\mathbb R^3$ in metres per second, and $a\in\mathbb R^3$ in metres. In the selected chart, $(x_1,x_2,z)$ are Cartesian coordinates in metres, with $x=(x_1,x_2)$ horizontal and $z$ upward; $e_z$ is the upward unit vector.

Fix depth $h>0$ metres and horizontal periods $L_1,L_2>0$ metres, and define $\mathbb T^2_L:=\mathbb R^2/(L_1\mathbb Z\times L_2\mathbb Z)$. A field on this torus is interpreted through its periodic lift $\widetilde f(\widetilde x)=f([\widetilde x])$. For fields on products of this torus with $I$ and $[-h,0]$, $C^r$ means that the lifted field has continuous ordinary coordinate partial derivatives through total order $r$, with continuous one-sided extensions at $z=-h,0$. Define $\nabla_h:=(\partial_{x_1},\partial_{x_2})$ and $\Delta_h:=\partial_{x_1}^2+\partial_{x_2}^2$ on the lifts. The real first-order displacement coefficient is $\eta:\mathbb T^2_L\times I\to\mathbb R$, in metres, and the real velocity-potential coefficient is $\phi:\mathbb T^2_L\times[-h,0]\times I\to\mathbb R$, in metres squared per second; assume $\eta$ is at least $C^2$ and $\phi$ at least $C^3$ in this sense. Their coefficients are formal and unrestricted in amplitude. Define the fluid-velocity field $u:=\nabla\phi=(\partial_{x_1}\phi,\partial_{x_2}\phi,\partial_z\phi):\mathbb T^2_L\times[-h,0]\times I\to\mathbb R^3$, in metres per second, with no added uniform velocity component. Take constant density $\rho>0$ kilograms per cubic metre, downward gravitational acceleration $-g e_z$ with $g>0$ metres per second squared, and surface tension $\gamma>0$ newtons per metre. The selected model is the first-order capillary free-surface model of the Postulate titled “Linear capillary free-surface model”: its equations on the flat reference slab $\mathbb T^2_L\times(-h,0)$ are

$$\Delta_h\phi+\partial_z^2\phi=0\quad(-h<z<0),\qquad \partial_z\phi(x,-h,t)=0,$$

$$\partial_t\eta(x,t)=\partial_z\phi(x,0,t),\qquad \partial_t\phi(x,0,t)+g\eta(x,t)-\frac{\gamma}{\rho}\Delta_h\eta(x,t)=0.$$

Let $\mathbb C:=\mathbb R[X]/(X^2+1)$, with $i:=[X]$ and $i^2=-1$; this quotient is the complex field. Let $\exp:\mathbb C\to\mathbb C$ be the everywhere-convergent series-defined complex exponential $\exp w:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}w^n/n!$. Let $\pi$ be twice the least positive zero of cosine. For $m=(m_1,m_2)\in\mathbb Z^2\setminus\{(0,0)\}$ define $\mathbf k:=2\pi(m_1/L_1,m_2/L_2)$ in inverse metres and $k:=|\mathbf k|>0$. For $\omega\in\mathbb C$ in inverse seconds, define on the quotient torus
$$q_m([x],t):=\exp\bigl(i(\mathbf k\cdot\widetilde x-\omega t)\bigr),$$
where $\widetilde x$ is any representative of $[x]$. Changing representatives changes the exponent by $2\pi iN$ for an integer $N$; the exponential addition law and $\exp(i\pi)=-1$ give $\exp(2\pi iN)=1$, so $q_m$ is well-defined. Its lift is smooth and satisfies $\Delta_hq_m=-k^2q_m$.

A nonzero complex mode of angular frequency $\omega$ and index $m$ is a pair $\eta_c:\mathbb T^2_L\times I\to\mathbb C$ and $\phi_c:\mathbb T^2_L\times[-h,0]\times I\to\mathbb C$ given by $\eta_c([x],t)=Hq_m([x],t)$ and $\phi_c([x],z,t)=F(z)q_m([x],t)$, satisfying the complex-linear extension of the displayed equations, where $H\in\mathbb C\setminus\{0\}$ is in metres and $F\in C^2([-h,0],\mathbb C)$ is in metres squared per second. Here $F$ is continuous on the closed interval, twice continuously differentiable on $(-h,0)$, and its first two derivatives extend continuously to both endpoints. The real and imaginary parts of every such mode solve the real linear model. Such a nonzero mode exists exactly when
$$\omega^2=\left(gk+\frac{\gamma}{\rho}k^3\right)\tanh(kh).$$
For these hypotheses the right-hand side is positive because $k,h,g,\gamma,\rho>0$ and $\tanh(kh)>0$. Thus each $m\ne(0,0)$ admits modes at the two real angular frequencies $\omega=\pm\sqrt{(gk+(\gamma/\rho)k^3)\tanh(kh)}$, with the positive real square root. This is a conditional prediction of the stated first-order model, not a measurement, a finite-amplitude approximation claim, or an assertion that an actual fluid satisfies every assumption.

items.title: Positive gravity and capillary modal restoring terms
items.design_state: Step 1 complete draft; readiness recorded separately.
items.statement:
Use $\mathbb C:=\mathbb R[X]/(X^2+1)$ with $i:=[X]$, the series-defined complex exponential $\exp w:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}w^n/n!$, and $\pi$ defined as twice the least positive zero of cosine.

Fix periods $L_1,L_2>0$ metres and let $\mathbb T^2_L:=\mathbb R^2/(L_1\mathbb Z\times L_2\mathbb Z)$. Define horizontal derivatives by differentiating the $L$-periodic lift to $\mathbb R^2$, and set $\Delta_h:=\partial_{x_1}^2+\partial_{x_2}^2$. Fix an integer lattice mode $m=(m_1,m_2)\in\mathbb Z^2\setminus\{(0,0)\}$ and define its wavevector and magnitude by $\mathbf k:=2\pi(m_1/L_1,m_2/L_2)$ in inverse metres and $k:=|\mathbf k|>0$. For any representative $\widetilde x\in\mathbb R^2$ of $[x]\in\mathbb T^2_L$, define the horizontal mode factor $q_m^h([x]):=\exp(i\mathbf k\cdot\widetilde x)$. A change of representative by $(L_1n_1,L_2n_2)$ changes its exponent by $2\pi iN$, where $N=m_1n_1+m_2n_2\in\mathbb Z$; the exponential addition law and $\exp(i\pi)=-1$ give $\exp(2\pi iN)=1$ for every integer $N$ (by repeated addition for $N\ge0$ and $\exp(w)\exp(-w)=1$ for $N<0$), so $q_m^h$ is well-defined. The identity $\exp(i\mathbf k\cdot\widetilde x)\exp(-i\mathbf k\cdot\widetilde x)=\exp(0)=1$ also shows $q_m^h$ never vanishes. Its periodic lift has $\Delta_hq_m^h=-k^2q_m^h$. Thus, for any unrestricted nonzero formal coefficient amplitude $H\in\mathbb C$ in metres, the nonzero horizontal mode $\eta_m:=Hq_m^h$ satisfies $\Delta_h\eta_m=-k^2\eta_m$. For real $s$, write $e^s:=\exp(s)$ and define $\sinh s:=(e^s-e^{-s})/2$, $\cosh s:=(e^s+e^{-s})/2$, and $\tanh s:=\sinh s/\cosh s$. Fix $h,\rho,g,\gamma>0$, where $h$ is depth in metres, $\rho$ is constant liquid mass density in kilograms per cubic metre, $g$ is the magnitude of the downward gravitational acceleration $-g e_z$ in metres per second squared, and $\gamma$ is the constant surface-tension coefficient in newtons per metre; $e_z$ is the upward unit vector. The vertical coordinate $z$ is upward, with the flat reference surface at $z=0$ and the fixed bed at $z=-h$. Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be the model's nonempty open time interval in seconds. The adopted first-order model is the one specified in the Postulate titled “Linear capillary free-surface model.” Its real coefficient fields are $\eta:\mathbb T^2_L\times I\to\mathbb R$ in metres and $\phi:\mathbb T^2_L\times[-h,0]\times I\to\mathbb R$ in metres squared per second; in periodic-lift coordinates they have continuous partial derivatives through total orders two and three, respectively, with one-sided continuous extensions at $z=-h,0$. Its equations in the selected periodic cell are $\Delta_h\phi+\partial_z^2\phi=0$ for $-h<z<0$, $\partial_z\phi(x,-h,t)=0$, $\partial_t\eta(x,t)=\partial_z\phi(x,0,t)$, and $\partial_t\phi(x,0,t)+g\eta(x,t)-\frac{\gamma}{\rho}\Delta_h\eta(x,t)=0$. For $\omega\in\mathbb C$ in inverse seconds define $q_m([x],t):=q_m^h([x])\exp(-i\omega t)$ for $t\in I$. A nonzero complex mode at index $m$ and angular frequency $\omega$ is a pair of fields $\eta_c:\mathbb T^2_L\times I\to\mathbb C$ and $\phi_c:\mathbb T^2_L\times[-h,0]\times I\to\mathbb C$ given by $\eta_c([x],t)=Hq_m([x],t)$ and $\phi_c([x],z,t)=F(z)q_m([x],t)$ and satisfying the complex-linear extension of those equations, with $H\in\mathbb C\setminus\{0\}$ in metres and $F\in C^2([-h,0],\mathbb C)$ in metres squared per second; here $F$ is continuous on $[-h,0]$, twice continuously differentiable on $(-h,0)$, and its first two derivatives extend continuously to the endpoints. The mode definition and dispersion result are those of the theorem titled “Linear capillary-gravity wave dispersion.” Its frequency relation is $\omega^2=(gk+(\gamma/\rho)k^3)\tanh(kh)>0$, since $h,k,g,\gamma,\rho>0$ and $\tanh(kh)>0$. Thus the gravity coefficient $g$ and capillary coefficient $\gamma k^2/\rho$ are both positive, and their contributions enter additively in the modal factor $g+\gamma k^2/\rho$. No finite-displacement constraint is imposed on the formal coefficient: optional geometric displacements are scaled by a sufficiently small dimensionless factor on compact time windows as in the postulate. This is a symbolic conditional model example; it reports no observation or numerical measurement.
